[102, PDF page 9] Different crop planting methods can significantly alter the structure and richness of the soil microbial community.
[103, PDF page 9] The traditional monoculture cropping pattern often leads to the excessive proliferation of certain microbial species while inhibiting the growth of others, ultimately reducing the overall diversity of soil microbes (Kunguang et al., 2024).
[104, PDF page 9] In contrast, plant root exudates can promote the growth of beneficial microbes in the soil, thereby increasing microbial diversity (Agarwal et al., 2023).
[105, PDF page 9] Furthermore, specific crop planting patterns may lead to a decline in certain functional microbes, which can diminish the ecosystem functions of the soil.
[106, PDF page 9] Conversely, diversified planting patterns can enhance the diversity of soil microbes and contribute to the stability and health of the soil ecosystem.
[107, PDF page 9] Different crop plantings can lead to alterations in the diversity and structure of the soil microbial community, thereby influencing the stability and function of the soil ecosystem (Hartmann and Six, 2023).
[108, PDF page 9] Notably, significant variations exist in how different crops affect soil microbes.
[109, PDF page 9] For instance, crops such as corn, wheat, and soybeans exert a more substantial impact on soil microbial diversity, whereas crops like rice and cotton have a relatively lesser influence.
[110, PDF page 9] The differences in growth cycles, along with the types and quantities of root exudates produced by various crops, significantly affect the growth, reproduction, and metabolic activities of soil microbes (Iannucci et al., 2021).
[111, PDF page 9] Additionally, the high nutrient requirements of crops can intensify competition for specific nutrients in the soil, consequently affecting the structure and function of the soil microbial community.
[112, PDF page 9] The root exudates and rhizosphere substances released by crop roots play a crucial role in influencing the growth and metabolism of soil microbes, thereby impacting soil microbial diversity.
[113, PDF page 9] Furthermore, the distinct root morphology and structure of different crops can lead to changes in the distribution and abundance of microbes within the soil, ultimately affecting the diversity of the soil microbial community (Zhou et al., 2022).
[114, PDF page 9] The excessive application of fertilizers can lead to the overgrowth of specific microbial populations in the soil, adversely affecting the survival and reproduction of other microbial communities, ultimately resulting in a reduction of microbial diversity (ˇSimanský et al., 2024).
[115, PDF page 9] Traditional tillage practices may compromise soil structure and diminish both the quantity and variety of soil microbes (Gupta et al., 2022).
[116, PDF page 9] In contrast, no-till or reduced-tillage practices can help to preserve soil microbial diversity.
[117, PDF page 9] Furthermore, the implementation of cover crops and crop rotation can enhance soil microbial diversity while maintaining the balance of soil nutrients.

claim.source_section_context:
[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 1. Introduction
[10, PDF page 1] Sustainable agriculture is critical in addressing the growing chal lenges of food security, environmental degradation, and climate change.
[11, PDF page 1] At the core of this sustainability lies the intricate relationship between soil and crops, a dynamic interaction that dictates crop productivity, soil health, and ecosystem resilience.
[12, PDF page 1] Understanding and optimizing these crop-soil synergies is essential for enhancing agricultural production and promoting long-term sustainability.
[13, PDF page 1] Soil health, characterized by its physical, chemical, and biological properties, plays a foundational role in determining crop performance.
[14, PDF page 1] Edaphic factors such as soil texture, moisture content, pH, and nutrient levels, all directly impact crop growth and development (Hu et al., 2024).
[15, PDF page 1] Sandy soils are particularly vulnerable to drought due to their poor water retention, while acidic soils can limit the growth of certain crops (Naorem et al., 2023).
[16, PDF page 1] Crop root systems play a vital role in enhancing soil structure, promoting the formation of soil aggregates, * Corresponding author.
[17, PDF page 1] E-mail address: wangxiukang@126.com (X.
[18, PDF page 1] This is an Safety 289 (2025) 117703 ScienceDirect www.elsevier.com/locate/ecoenv b ’an, Shaanxi 716000, China and improving soil aeration and water-holding capacity (Lu et al., 2020).
[19, PDF page 1] Additionally, these root systems recruit beneficial microorgan- - isms that help maintain the balance of the soil ecosystem (Han et al., 2021).
[20, PDF page 1] Equally important is the role of soil biodiversity, particularly the rhizosphere microbial communities, which are vital in nutrient cycling processes like nitrogen fixation and phosphate solubilization (Saeed et al., 2021).
[21, PDF page 1] Soil bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes establish a symbiotic relationship with crop roots, facilitating nutrient absorption, enhancing disease resistance, and aiding in the decomposition of organic matter (Wei et al., 2024).
[22, PDF page 1] These microorganisms not only support crop nutrition but also contribute to stress tolerance and disease resistance, providing a natural buffer against environmental stresses.
[23, PDF page 1] This synergy between crop-soil-microbes promotes nutrient cycling and contribute to the overall soil ecosystem stability.
[24, PDF page 2] Different crops have different ability to absorb and use soil nutrients.
[25, PDF page 2] Selecting suitable crop varieties for rotation and intercropping can improve soil fertility and health (Glaze-Corcoran et al., 2020).
[26, PDF page 2] Diverse planting methods can promote soil microbial diversity, thereby maintaining the balance and stability of the soil ecosystem (Gupta et al., 2022).
[27, PDF page 2] Additionally, the nutrient supply, water retention, and aeration conditions within the soil significantly impact crop growth and yield (Zhang et al., 2022c).
[28, PDF page 2] The development of crop root systems is intricately linked to the soil’s structural looseness or compactness, with soil microorganisms playing a crucial regulatory role in root system growth (Sharma et al., 2021).
[29, PDF page 2] The soil microbial community contributes to crop growth and development through the decomposition of organic matter, nitrogen fixation, and the facilitation of nutrient cycling (Yadav et al., 2021).

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 1. Introduction.

[LOCAL SECTION HEADING] 1. Introduction
[10, PDF page 1] Sustainable agriculture is critical in addressing the growing chal lenges of food security, environmental degradation, and climate change.
[11, PDF page 1] At the core of this sustainability lies the intricate relationship between soil and crops, a dynamic interaction that dictates crop productivity, soil health, and ecosystem resilience.
[12, PDF page 1] Understanding and optimizing these crop-soil synergies is essential for enhancing agricultural production and promoting long-term sustainability.
[13, PDF page 1] Soil health, characterized by its physical, chemical, and biological properties, plays a foundational role in determining crop performance.
[14, PDF page 1] Edaphic factors such as soil texture, moisture content, pH, and nutrient levels, all directly impact crop growth and development (Hu et al., 2024).
[15, PDF page 1] Sandy soils are particularly vulnerable to drought due to their poor water retention, while acidic soils can limit the growth of certain crops (Naorem et al., 2023).
[16, PDF page 1] Crop root systems play a vital role in enhancing soil structure, promoting the formation of soil aggregates, * Corresponding author.

[19, PDF page 1] Additionally, these root systems recruit beneficial microorgan- - isms that help maintain the balance of the soil ecosystem (Han et al., 2021).
[20, PDF page 1] Equally important is the role of soil biodiversity, particularly the rhizosphere microbial communities, which are vital in nutrient cycling processes like nitrogen fixation and phosphate solubilization (Saeed et al., 2021).
[21, PDF page 1] Soil bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes establish a symbiotic relationship with crop roots, facilitating nutrient absorption, enhancing disease resistance, and aiding in the decomposition of organic matter (Wei et al., 2024).
[22, PDF page 1] These microorganisms not only support crop nutrition but also contribute to stress tolerance and disease resistance, providing a natural buffer against environmental stresses.
[23, PDF page 1] This synergy between crop-soil-microbes promotes nutrient cycling and contribute to the overall soil ecosystem stability.
[24, PDF page 2] Different crops have different ability to absorb and use soil nutrients.
[25, PDF page 2] Selecting suitable crop varieties for rotation and intercropping can improve soil fertility and health (Glaze-Corcoran et al., 2020).
[26, PDF page 2] Diverse planting methods can promote soil microbial diversity, thereby maintaining the balance and stability of the soil ecosystem (Gupta et al., 2022).
[27, PDF page 2] Additionally, the nutrient supply, water retention, and aeration conditions within the soil significantly impact crop growth and yield (Zhang et al., 2022c).
[28, PDF page 2] The development of crop root systems is intricately linked to the soil’s structural looseness or compactness, with soil microorganisms playing a crucial regulatory role in root system growth (Sharma et al., 2021).

[30, PDF page 2] Concurrently, root exudates secreted by crop root systems can attract soil microorganisms, fostering a symbiotic relationship that enhances microbial diversity and abundance.
[31, PDF page 2] Gaining a deeper understanding of the interactive relationship between crops and soil microorganisms is essential for optimizing the soil environment and enhancing crop yield.
[32, PDF page 2] Despite the critical importance of these interactions, current research often focuses on isolated aspects such as root growth, nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance.

[34, PDF page 2] Unlike previous reviews that predominantly address either chemical or biological facets (Sela et al., 2024), this work explores the synergies among crop genotypes, soil properties, and microbial communities.

[36, PDF page 2] Thus, this review aims to explore the multifaceted interactions between crops and soils, focusing on how these dynamics influence soil health and agricultural sustainability.
[37, PDF page 2] By synthesizing knowledge on microbial interactions, soil management practices, and advanced precision agriculture technologies, we provide insights into optimizing soil-crop-microbial synergies.
[38, PDF page 2] The ultimate goal is to create resilient agricultural practices that enhance productivity, conserve soil resources, and contribute to global efforts toward sustainable development.

fragments: This study examined how variations in tillage intensity and fertilization shape soil microbial communities and, through these shifts, affect the nutritional quality of maize and wheat.

Soil microbial diversity and functional potential were assessed through metagenomic sequencing, while grain content was determined using standardized biochemical assays. <italic> <bold>Results</bold> </italic> : Within long-term trial contexts, it was demonstrated that tillage–fertilization combinations modulate soil microbiomes in ways that propagate to grain nutritional quality.

Balanced fertilization was associated with denser, better-connected microbial networks, while excessive inputs disrupted ecological equilibrium and weakened the translation of soil functions to nutritional traits. Conclusions : Crop nutritional quality can be tuned via the soil microbiome: under moderated inputs, ploughing tends to raise carotenoids/lipophilic antioxidants, whereas deep loosening with balanced fertilization favors water-soluble antioxidants; excessive fertilization disrupts microbial balance and weakens these benefits.

[36, PDF page 6] Furthermore, crops with different root exudates support a more diverse and functional soil microbial community (Zhou et al., 2023).
[37, PDF page 6] This microbial diversity is crucial for nutrient cycling, as various microorganisms specialize in decomposing different organic matter components and mobilizing nutrients for plant uptake.
[38, PDF page 6] Additionally, a diverse microbial community can suppress soil pathogens through competitive exclusion and the production of antimicrobial compounds, thereby reducing the incidence of soil-borne diseases (Tian et al., 2022).
[39, PDF page 6] The presence of multiple plant species also disrupts the life cycles of pests and pathogens, making it harder for them to establish and proliferate.
[40, PDF page 6] Crop diversity also contributes to the resilience of the soil ecosystem by enhancing nutrient use efficiency.

[42, PDF page 6] This complementary nutrient usage ensures a more balanced and sustainable nutrient profile in the soil.
[43, PDF page 6] Moreover, diverse root systems create a more heterogeneous soil environment, which supports a wider range of soil organisms, including beneficial bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates.
[44, PDF page 6] These organisms play vital roles in maintaining soil health by decomposing organic matter, promoting soil aggregation, and improving soil structure.
[45, PDF page 6] The synergistic interactions between diverse plant roots and soil microorganisms promote the formation of stable soil aggregates, which enhance soil structure and resilience against physical disturbances.
[46, PDF page 6] These aggregates improve soil aeration and water infiltration while reducing compaction, thereby creating a more conducive environment for root growth and microbial activity.
[47, PDF page 6] Specifically, crop root systems enhance soil porosity by creating macropores that facilitate water and air movement, and increase aggregate stability by binding soil particles with root exudates and fungal hyphae, leading to a 15–25 % increase in mean weight diameter of aggregates and a 10–20 % increase in porosity in the root zone (C ́arceles Rodríguez et al., 2022).
[48, PDF page 6] Additionally, diverse plant residues provide a continuous supply of organic material for decomposition, ensuring a steady release of nutrients and maintaining soil organic matter levels.

[50, PDF page 6] This microbial diversity enhances the soil’s ability to recover from disturbances, such as drought or pest outbreaks, by ensuring that multiple functional groups are available to respond to changes in environmental conditions.
[51, PDF page 6] Consequently, crop diversity significantly influences soil health and the resilience of the agricultural ecosystem.
[52, PDF page 6] By judiciously employing diverse planting methods, it is possible to enhance farmland productivity and ecological stability, thereby achieving sustainable agricultural development.
[53, PDF page 6] Future agricultural production should place greater emphasis on the role of crop diversity in promoting soil health and ecosystem resilience, while continuously fostering the healthy development of the agricultural ecosystem.

[29, PDF page 5] Selecting an appropriate crop planting structure and implementing crop rotation and intercropping can effectively reduce the depletion of specific nutrients in the soil while minimizing the incidence of soil-borne diseases and pests.
[30, PDF page 5] The judicious application of both chemical and organic fertilizers helps to balance the nutrient content in the soil, ensuring that crops receive the necessary nutrients for optimal growth (Bhunia et al., 2021).
[31, PDF page 5] In addition to these practices, crop diversity enhances soil resilience through various underlying mechanisms.
[32, PDF page 5] Diverse cropping systems introduce a range of root architectures and depths, which improve soil structure and texture, increase soil permeability, and Fig. 2.
[33, PDF page 5] Ecological service effects of crop diversity on soil health.

[35, PDF page 6] These structural improvements facilitate better water infiltration and retention, thereby reducing the risk of erosion and improving the soil’s ability to withstand extreme weather conditions.
[36, PDF page 6] Furthermore, crops with different root exudates support a more diverse and functional soil microbial community (Zhou et al., 2023).
[37, PDF page 6] This microbial diversity is crucial for nutrient cycling, as various microorganisms specialize in decomposing different organic matter components and mobilizing nutrients for plant uptake.
[38, PDF page 6] Additionally, a diverse microbial community can suppress soil pathogens through competitive exclusion and the production of antimicrobial compounds, thereby reducing the incidence of soil-borne diseases (Tian et al., 2022).
[39, PDF page 6] The presence of multiple plant species also disrupts the life cycles of pests and pathogens, making it harder for them to establish and proliferate.
[40, PDF page 6] Crop diversity also contributes to the resilience of the soil ecosystem by enhancing nutrient use efficiency.
[41, PDF page 6] Different crops have varying nutrient requirements and uptake patterns, which prevents the monopolization of specific nutrients and reduces the likelihood of nutrient depletion.
[42, PDF page 6] This complementary nutrient usage ensures a more balanced and sustainable nutrient profile in the soil.
[43, PDF page 6] Moreover, diverse root systems create a more heterogeneous soil environment, which supports a wider range of soil organisms, including beneficial bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates.
[44, PDF page 6] These organisms play vital roles in maintaining soil health by decomposing organic matter, promoting soil aggregation, and improving soil structure.
[45, PDF page 6] The synergistic interactions between diverse plant roots and soil microorganisms promote the formation of stable soil aggregates, which enhance soil structure and resilience against physical disturbances.
[46, PDF page 6] These aggregates improve soil aeration and water infiltration while reducing compaction, thereby creating a more conducive environment for root growth and microbial activity.
[47, PDF page 6] Specifically, crop root systems enhance soil porosity by creating macropores that facilitate water and air movement, and increase aggregate stability by binding soil particles with root exudates and fungal hyphae, leading to a 15–25 % increase in mean weight diameter of aggregates and a 10–20 % increase in porosity in the root zone (C ́arceles Rodríguez et al., 2022).
[48, PDF page 6] Additionally, diverse plant residues provide a continuous supply of organic material for decomposition, ensuring a steady release of nutrients and maintaining soil organic matter levels.
[49, PDF page 6] Variations in root exudates and residue composition among different plant species not only provide additional substrates for soil microorganisms but also create niches for a diverse array of microbial taxa (Zha et al., 2022).
[50, PDF page 6] This microbial diversity enhances the soil’s ability to recover from disturbances, such as drought or pest outbreaks, by ensuring that multiple functional groups are available to respond to changes in environmental conditions.
[51, PDF page 6] Consequently, crop diversity significantly influences soil health and the resilience of the agricultural ecosystem.
[52, PDF page 6] By judiciously employing diverse planting methods, it is possible to enhance farmland productivity and ecological stability, thereby achieving sustainable agricultural development.
[53, PDF page 6] Future agricultural production should place greater emphasis on the role of crop diversity in promoting soil health and ecosystem resilience, while continuously fostering the healthy development of the agricultural ecosystem.

[6] In the context of climate change, biodiversity loss, and intensifying land use, improving soil health has emerged as a nature-based solution to enhance food security while mitigating environmental and climate-related risks.
[7] This Research Topic, Health, was developed to explore the interconnected relationships between soil properties, crop nutritional quality, and human health outcomes.
[8] The Research Topic brings together original research and review articles that examine how soil management practices, such as balanced nutrient inputs, organic amendments, microbial interventions, and climateadaptive strategies, can enhance soil functionality and crop nutritional profiles.
[9] The studies brought together in this Research Topic collectively tell this deeper story, one in which soil health emerges as a central protagonist in the global quest for food quality, nutritional security, and human wellbeing.
[10] The story begins in the highly weathered soils of Sub-Saharan Africa, where sulfur, often overlooked in fertilizer regimes, quietly governs both soil fertility and the nutritional value of staple crops. deficiency is not merely a soil constraint but a nutritional bottleneck, linking soil degradation directly to hidden hunger.

[19, PDF page 2] In doing so, it reframes soil management as a frontline defense for public health, not merely an agronomic intervention.
[20, PDF page 2] Measuring and safeguarding crop quality, however, requires tools that can keep pace with the complexity of soil–plant interactions.

[22, PDF page 2] Their study bridges the gap between soil management and food composition, enabling rapid evaluation of nutritional outcomes that were once costly and time-consuming to measure.
[23, PDF page 2] This technological advance strengthens our ability to translate soil health into tangible improvements in food quality.
[24, PDF page 2] The narrative deepens further into the living soil, where biological diversity shapes plant health in profound ways.
[25, PDF page 2] Amrutha Lakshmi et al. demonstrate how Trichoderma species suppress Ganoderma-induced basal stem rot in oil palm, offering mechanistic insights into microbial-based disease control.
[26, PDF page 2] Their findings reinforce the idea that resilient soils, rich in beneficial microbes, can protect crops naturally, reducing dependence on chemical inputs while sustaining long-term productivity.
[27, PDF page 2] The story comes full circle with Chandel et al., who disentangle the role of native soil microbes in enhancing both soil health parameters and the accumulation of nutritionally valuable phytochemicals in Aloe vera.
[28, PDF page 2] This work vividly illustrates the soil–microbe–plant nexus, showing how invisible biological communities beneath our feet shape the nutritional and functional quality of crops consumed by humans.
[29, PDF page 2] Together, the articles in this Research Topic demonstrate that soil health is not merely an agronomic concern but a key determinant of food quality, food safety, and human nutrition.
[30, PDF page 2] By integrating perspectives from soil science, agronomy, microbiology, plant nutrition, and public health, this Research Topic underscores the need for holistic, systems-based approaches to agricultural management.
[31, PDF page 2] We hope this Research Topic will stimulate interdisciplinary research, inform sustainable land-use policies, and encourage the adoption of soil management practices that enhance crop nutritional quality and support human health.

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses biofortification (genetic/nutrient enhancement of crops) and its effects on nutrient deficiency and malnutrition, but does not examine soil management practices (balanced nutrient inputs, organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) as a means of enhancing crop nutritional profiles. The upstream edge is therefore not addressed by this paper. The shared entity 'crop nutritional quality' is a compatible conceptual junction, but the paper provides no evidence linking soil management to that entity, so the local connection remains unresolved.

edge_findings.reason: Paper links improved crop nutrient content (biofortification) to reduced nutrient deficiencies and improved health, supporting the general crop-quality-to-malnutrition link, but does not address reduced quality from degraded soils.

Paper discusses biofortification and genetic engineering to improve crop nutritional profiles, not soil management practices (balanced nutrient inputs, organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies). No evidence on the claimed soil-to-crop-nutrition pathway.

connection_findings.reason: Shared entity 'crop nutritional quality' is conceptually compatible, but the paper provides no evidence that soil management practices enhance it, so the upstream-to-junction link is unestablished.

fragments: One possible way to address nutrient deficiency and combat malnutrition is through biofortification.
Biofortification is a promising strategy for enhancing the nutritional condition of at-risk populations.

The health conditions of people have been shown to improve and nutrient deficiencies were reduced when biofortified crops were grown. Particularly in environments with limited resources, biofortification showed considerable promise as a long-term and economical solution to nutrient shortages and malnutrition.
proofs.quoted_span: One possible way to address nutrient deficiency and combat malnutrition is through biofortification. [NON-ADJACENT CONTEXT] Biofortification is a promising strategy for enhancing the nutritional condition of at-risk populations. [NON-ADJACENT CONTEXT] The health conditions of people have been shown to improve and nutrient deficiencies were reduced when biofortified crops were grown. Particularly in environments with limited resources, biofortification showed considerable promise as a long-term and economical solution to nutrient shortages and malnutrition.

paper.title: Biofortification as a solution for addressing nutrient deficiencies and malnutrition
paper.independence_group: bibliography:biofortification as a solution for addressing nutrient deficiencies and malnutrition|bindu naik|2024

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses biofortification/breeding for micronutrient content and its potential to reduce micronutrient malnutrition, but does not test soil management practices as a route to enhanced crop nutritional profiles. Edge 1 is only broadly contextual; edge 2 is partially addressed because the paper links low staple-crop micronutrient content to widespread deficiencies, though it frames malnutrition as primarily a symptom of poverty and does not establish the full causal claim. The shared node (crop nutritional quality) is compatible in topic, but the local chain is not directly demonstrated.

edge_findings.reason: Paper discusses breeding/biofortification and fertiliser/irrigation as breeding context, not soil management practices (balanced nutrients, organic amendments, microbial interventions) enhancing crop nutritional profiles.

Paper links micronutrient deficiencies in staple crops to malnutrition affecting over 2 billion people, supporting the general direction, but frames malnutrition primarily as a symptom of poverty and does not establish the specific causal claim about reduced crop nutritional quality increasing malnutrition risk.

connection_findings.reason: Shared node is crop nutritional quality; paper supports the quality-to-malnutrition side but does not establish that soil management practices raise crop nutritional quality, so the junction is not demonstrated.

fragments: Breeding for benign agro-ecological conditions is relatively easy since many environmental and biotic stress factors are less important than in less favoured areas, partly due to the use of inputs such as fertilisers and irrigation. Therefore, breeding for reducing nutrient deficiencies for the urban poor may be relatively straightforward.
proofs.quoted_span: Breeding for benign agro-ecological conditions is relatively easy since many environmental and biotic stress factors are less important than in less favoured areas, partly due to the use of inputs such as fertilisers and irrigation. Therefore, breeding for reducing nutrient deficiencies for the urban poor may be relatively straightforward.

fragments: Deficiencies, particularly of iron, zinc, iodine and vitamin A, limit the well-being and productivity of over 2 billion people worldwide. Micronutrient malnutrition is primarily a sympton of poverty and thus tends to decline with improvements in livelihoods. Targeted strategies available to alleviate micronutrient deficiencies include dietary diversification, food fortification, supplementation, and more recently breeding of agricultural crops for higher nutrient levels (or ‘bio-fortification’).
proofs.quoted_span: Deficiencies, particularly of iron, zinc, iodine and vitamin A, limit the well-being and productivity of over 2 billion people worldwide. Micronutrient malnutrition is primarily a sympton of poverty and thus tends to decline with improvements in livelihoods. Targeted strategies available to alleviate micronutrient deficiencies include dietary diversification, food fortification, supplementation, and more recently breeding of agricultural crops for higher nutrient levels (or ‘bio-fortification’).

fragments: Approximately half of the iron and zinc intake in Asia is accounted for by the staple crops, rice and wheat. Doubling the content (and bioavailability) in these staples can potentially solve the majority of deficiencies without changing the food habits.
proofs.quoted_span: Approximately half of the iron and zinc intake in Asia is accounted for by the staple crops, rice and wheat. Doubling the content (and bioavailability) in these staples can potentially solve the majority of deficiencies without changing the food habits.

paper.title: Breeding crops to reduce micronutrient malnutrition
paper.independence_group: bibliography:breeding crops to reduce micronutrient malnutrition|n p louwaars|2003

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses pollinator dependence of micronutrient-rich crops and overlaps with human micronutrient deficiency, not soil management practices enhancing crop nutritional profiles. The upstream claim is not addressed; the shared node 'crop nutritional quality' is a related but differently framed concept, so the local junction is unresolved rather than supported or contradicted.

edge_findings.reason: Paper links pollination dependence to micronutrient deficiency risk, not reduced crop nutritional quality as a cause of malnutrition; different driver and no causal test of crop-quality reduction.

Paper examines pollination dependence of crop micronutrient content and deficiency overlap; it does not test soil management practices (nutrient inputs, organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) or their enhancement of crop nutritional profiles.

connection_findings.reason: Shared node is crop nutritional quality, but the paper's evidence concerns pollinator dependence of micronutrient content, not soil-management-driven enhancement feeding into malnutrition risk; no local compatibility established.

paper.title: Global malnutrition overlaps with pollinator-dependent micronutrient production
paper.independence_group: bibliography:global malnutrition overlaps with pollinator dependent micronutrient production|rebecca chaplin kramer|2014

paper_assessments.finding: The paper supports the general link between soil fertility/fertilization and crop micronutrient density, and between poor nutritional quality and malnutrition, but does not address the full breadth of the upstream claim (organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) or the specific causal malnutrition-risk wording of the downstream claim. The shared node 'crop nutritional quality' is compatible across both edges.

edge_findings.reason: Paper establishes soil micronutrient status/fertilization and amendments affect crop micronutrient density, supporting the fertilization/amendment part; organic amendments, microbial interventions and climate-adaptive strategies are not all addressed, so partial.

Paper states that if agriculture cannot supply essential nutrients, malnutrition develops, and that crop nutritional quality must be a priority to reduce malnutrition prevalence; supports the direction but frames it as nutrient supply/quality rather than explicitly 'increased risks'.

connection_findings.reason: Both edges concern crop nutritional/micronutrient quality as the intermediate; upstream improves it and downstream loss of it contributes to malnutrition, consistent shared node.

fragments: 3.3 Soil fertility/Fertilization In general, well-nourished crops grown on fertile soils have higher micronutrient density in edible portions than nutrient-stressed crops grown on infertile soils (Welch, 1998; Welch, 2001).
Thus, soil micronutrient status and soil amendments are important factors that impact the micronutrient output of these systems.
Levels of available micronutrients in soils are an important factor in determining micronutrient content of crops (Allaway, 1986; Welch and Graham, 2005).
proofs.quoted_span: 3.3 Soil fertility/Fertilization In general, well-nourished crops grown on fertile soils have higher micronutrient density in edible portions than nutrient-stressed crops grown on infertile soils (Welch, 1998; Welch, 2001). [NON-ADJACENT CONTEXT] Thus, soil micronutrient status and soil amendments are important factors that impact the micronutrient output of these systems. [NON-ADJACENT CONTEXT] Levels of available micronutrients in soils are an important factor in determining micronutrient content of crops (Allaway, 1986; Welch and Graham, 2005).

fragments: Macronutrient fertilizers (e.g., fertilizers that contain nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, calcium and/or magnesium), and soil amendments, such as lime, gypsum and organic matter, can affect the available forms of micronutrients in soils and the concentrations of micronutrients in crops grown on them (Allaway, 1986; Grunes and Allaway, 1985).
However, amending soils with lime may reduce the uptake of certain micronutrients including zinc, copper, iron, and cobalt, and increase the uptake of selenium and molybdenum.
proofs.quoted_span: Macronutrient fertilizers (e.g., fertilizers that contain nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus, sulfur, calcium and/or magnesium), and soil amendments, such as lime, gypsum and organic matter, can affect the available forms of micronutrients in soils and the concentrations of micronutrients in crops grown on them (Allaway, 1986; Grunes and Allaway, 1985). [NON-ADJACENT CONTEXT] However, amending soils with lime may reduce the uptake of certain micronutrients including zinc, copper, iron, and cobalt, and increase the uptake of selenium and molybdenum.

fragments: If agriculture cannot supply all the essential nutrients in amounts required for good health and productive lives, malnutrition develops.
Increasing yields is important but the nutritional quality of crops produced must also be a priority if sustainable progress toward reducing the prevalence of malnutrition is to be realized.
proofs.quoted_span: If agriculture cannot supply all the essential nutrients in amounts required for good health and productive lives, malnutrition develops. fragments: Micronutrient malnutrition affects a third to a half of the global population. It causes untold human suffering and levies huge costs on society in terms of unrealized human potential and lost economic productivity.
proofs.quoted_span: Micronutrient malnutrition affects a third to a half of the global population. It causes untold human suffering and levies huge costs on society in terms of unrealized human potential and lost economic productivity.

paper.title: Food system strategies for preventing micronutrient malnutrition
paper.independence_group: bibliography:food system strategies for preventing micronutrient malnutrition|by dennis d miller|2013

paper_assessments.finding: The abstract of Miner (2020) cautions that claims linking soil-health management to crop quality and productivity need careful examination and that factors beyond soil-health metrics determine crop nutritional quality. It does not address malnutrition outcomes. Thus the upstream enhancement claim is only partially and cautiously addressed, while the downstream malnutrition link is not addressed.

edge_findings.reason: Paper discusses SH management and crop nutritional quality but explicitly says such claims merit careful examination and that non-SH factors determine quality; no specific practices or enhancement outcome established.
Abstract does not examine malnutrition or micronutrient deficiency outcomes of reduced crop nutritional quality.

connection_findings.reason: Shared node is crop nutritional quality, but paper treats SH-quality links cautiously and does not connect quality to malnutrition, so the junction is not established.

fragments: Abstract Globally, food systems face multiple challenges, including minimizing environmental impacts, adapting to a changing climate, increasing yields, and maintaining and/or increasing crop nutritional quality. Management techniques that focus on soil health (SH) are promising solutions to mitigate some environmental impacts and may increase economic returns. However, claims that SH increases will concurrently increase crop quality and productivity merit careful examination.
proofs.quoted_span: Abstract Globally, food systems face multiple challenges, including minimizing environmental impacts, adapting to a changing climate, increasing yields, and maintaining and/or increasing crop nutritional quality. Management techniques that focus on soil health (SH) are promising solutions to mitigate some environmental impacts and may increase economic returns. However, claims that SH increases will concurrently increase crop quality and productivity merit careful examination.

fragments: Factors beyond SH metrics determine crop nutritional quality.
proofs.quoted_span: Factors beyond SH metrics determine crop nutritional quality.

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses soil management effects on soil C/N and yields, not crop nutritional profiles or malnutrition; neither edge is substantiated, and the shared node 'crop nutritional quality' is not measured.

edge_findings.reason: Paper reviews tillage, cover crops and N fertilization effects on yields and soil C/N/leaching; no crop nutritional profile outcome.
No measure of reduced crop nutritional quality or malnutrition risk; only soil/water quality and yield outcomes.

connection_findings.reason: Shared node crop nutritional quality is not assessed by the paper, so the local link cannot be evaluated.

fragments: This paper reviews the findings of the effects of tillage practices, cover crops, and nitrogen (N) fertilization rates on crop yields, soil organic carbon (C) and N concentrations, and nitrate (NO3)-N leaching from the soil.

Management practices consisting of combinations of conservation tillage, mixture of legume and nonlegume cover crops, and reduced rate of N fertilization have the potentials for sustaining crop yields, increasing soil C and N storage, and reducing soil N leaching, thereby helping to improve soil and water qualities.

paper.independence_group: bibliography:agricultural management practices to sustain crop yields and improve soil and environmental qualities|upendra m sainju|2003

paper_assessments.finding: The paper addresses salinity effects on vegetable growth, nutrition and quality, and management practices to prevent salinization. It does not test the broad claim that soil management practices (balanced nutrients, organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) enhance crop nutritional profiles, nor does it establish that reduced crop nutritional quality increases malnutrition risk. The shared node 'crop nutritional quality' is discussed in a salinity context, but the two neighboring claims are not jointly supported.

edge_findings.reason: Paper concerns salinity/irrigation/fertilization management for vegetables; it does not test balanced nutrient inputs, organic amendments, microbial interventions or climate-adaptive strategies as enhancers of crop nutritional profiles.

Paper notes vegetables are important for nutrition and that micronutrient deficiencies relate to low vegetable intake, but does not establish that reduced crop nutritional quality contributes to increased malnutrition risk.

connection_findings.reason: Shared node is crop nutritional quality, but the paper provides no evidence linking the upstream soil-management enhancement to the downstream malnutrition outcome; the local connection is not established.

paper.title: Soil and Crop Management Practices to Minimize the Impact of Waterlogging on Crop Productivity
paper.independence_group: bibliography:soil and crop management practices to minimize the impact of waterlogging on crop productivity|s m nuruzzaman manik|2019

paper_assessments.finding: The paper supports the general direction of both links: agronomic soil/fertilizer management can raise crop nutrient content (though variably and with caveats), and malnutrition/micronutrient deficiencies are a major persistent problem in South Asia. However, the paper does not directly establish that soil management practices enhance crop nutritional profiles as a broad class, nor does it causally link reduced crop nutritional quality to increased malnutrition risk; it treats malnutrition as multifactorial (poverty, food prices, climate). The shared node 'crop nutritional quality' is compatible in compartment and direction, but the local connection is only partially substantiated.

edge_findings.reason: Paper states agronomic approaches (soil/fertilizer management, micronutrient-enriched fertilizers) enhance crop nutrient content, matching the practice-to-nutritional-profile direction, but addresses agronomic biofortification specifically rather than the full listed set (organic amendments, microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) and notes variable effectiveness.

Paper establishes malnutrition/micronutrient deficiency as a severe persistent challenge and that biofortification improves nutritional quality of staple foods, consistent with the link, but does not directly demonstrate that reduced crop nutritional quality causally increases malnutrition risk; malnutrition is framed as multifactorial.

connection_findings.reason: Both edges concern crop nutrient content/quality and its relation to malnutrition; the shared node is the same biological compartment (edible crop nutrient content) and directions are consistent, though the paper does not test the full chain.

fragments: Agronomic approaches enhance the nutrient content of crops primarily through soil and fertilizer management. This includes applying micronutrient-enriched fertilizers, optimizing soil fertility, and using foliar sprays to boost nutrient uptake and accumulation in edible plant parts [ 82 ].

This includes applying micronutrient-enriched fertilizers, optimizing soil fertility, and using foliar sprays to boost nutrient uptake and accumulation in edible plant parts [ 82 ].

fragments: Agronomic biofortification, primarily through micronutrient-enriched fertilizers, is an effective but variable strategy for boosting the nutrient content of crops.

fragments: Malnutrition remains one of the most persistent global public health challenges, despite notable progress in agriculture, healthcare, and socioeconomic development [ 1 ]. Its impact is particularly severe in South Asia, especially in India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and parts of China, where demographic pressures, economic disparities, and environmental stressors converge to exacerbate nutritional deficits [ 2 ].

fragments: Malnutrition remains a critical challenge in South Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and China, where micronutrient deficiencies in iron, zinc, and vitamin A disproportionately affect children, adolescent girls, pregnant women, and the elderly.

Biofortification offers a powerful tool to enhance the nutritional quality of staple foods, but its real potential lies in tailoring interventions to demographic needs and embedding them within existing policy frameworks.

connection_assessments.reason: Same intermediate crop micronutrient/nutritional quality links soil fertility/amendments to crop density upstream and inadequate nutrient supply/quality to malnutrition downstream.

edge_assessments.reason: Fertilization/soil amendments and farmyard manure shown to affect/increase crop micronutrient density, but microbial interventions and climate-adaptive strategies and balanced inputs breadth not established.

Failure to supply essential nutrients/nutritional quality linked to malnutrition development/prevalence, and staple micronutrient content linked to deficiencies; biofortification framing supports direction but not exact degraded-soil causal wording.

entity_roles.contextual_role: farming intervention applied to soil to improve fertility and crop nutrient density
entity_roles.reason: Fertilizers and amendments including organic matter shown to affect crop micronutrient concentrations.

entity_roles.contextual_role: intermediate crop micronutrient density/nutritional quality linking soil management to human nutrition
entity_roles.reason: Measured as micronutrient density/content and nutritional quality of crops/edible portions.

entity_roles.contextual_role: human malnutrition/micronutrient deficiency outcome from inadequate crop nutrient supply
entity_roles.reason: Malnutrition/micronutrient malnutrition affecting population health and productivity.

limitations: Upstream breadth (microbial interventions, climate-adaptive strategies) not evidenced; only fertilization/organic amendments supported.
Downstream evidence supports general nutrient-supply to malnutrition direction, not exact reduced-quality risk quantification.
Cautious review notes factors beyond soil health determine crop quality.
assessment_history.scope_reason: Soil management to crop composition/nutritional quality to human malnutrition falls within soil-crop-nutrient-health pathway including food composition mechanisms.
assessment_history.synthesis: Component evidence supports soil fertilization/amendments affecting crop micronutrient density and poor crop nutritional supply contributing to malnutrition, with compatible shared quality node, but neither claim is fully established in its broad wording so only partial component support.

connection_assessments.reason: Same compartment edible crop micronutrient/nutritional quality links soil fertility/amendments to malnutrition; directions consistent.

edge_assessments.reason: Multiple applicable supports show soil/fertilizer management and organic amendments raise crop nutrient/micronutrient content, but only subset of listed practices and variable effects; full broad claim unverified.

Applicable supports link crop nutritional/micronutrient quality and supply to malnutrition/micronutrient deficiency, but malnutrition framed as multifactorial and specific degraded-soil causal increase not directly tested.
